newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia's highway robbers terrorise truckers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia's highway robbers terrorise truckers.

text.p: It looks like a scene from the Wild West or the cinema saga of post-apocalypse highway hero Mad Max as long convoys of trucks, drivers with assault rifles and shotguns to hand, speed along snow-swept Russian roads.
They do not stop, for to do so can be deadly on the route from Russia's northwestern frontier to Moscow.
Danger lurks along the 600 km (400 mile) journey from the capital to St Petersburg and beyond into Finland.

Highly organised and heavily armed robbers -- modern day highwaymen -- are ready to make off with expensive cargoes of tobacco, alcohol, coffee or domestic electronic appliances. The lives of the drivers mean little to them.

"Western insurance companies only agree to work with the cargo before it crosses the Russian border," said a Brazilian coffee trader. "The rest depends on those who buy the product in the country. They have to organise security themselves."

Importers say banditry is hurting their businesses badly. Many cargoes disappear on the road, making importing big volumes of expensive products without proper insurance too risky for Russian firms' western partners.
"We may see a fall in Russian imports due to wide-scale robbery," the coffee trader said.
"Insurers worked in the Wild West and during wars. But now they say Russia is too much for them."

Much of Russia's imports, especially food and consumer goods, arrive via the Baltic, at Finnish ports or at St Petersburg, and are then transferred to Moscow and other cities in the interior by lorry.
EACH LOAD A TEMPTING TARGET

Each load represents a tempting target for the highway robbers. A container load of foreign cigarettes is worth more than $100,000. Coffee is popular too, but a bit cheaper at $70,000 per container, while electronics may fetch much, much more.
Yet the first in a series of dangers along the road awaits importers right at the customs yard on entry to Russia.

Importers and haulage firms complain that low-ranking, often poorly paid, customs officers regularly help themselves to "samples" of cargo, apparently with impunity, although officials have pledged to stamp out corruption.
"Customs officials normally take several boxes off each container. That is their business," said one Russian importer, who also declined to be named.
The Brazilian trader said, however, that major-league criminals posing as customs officials along the Moscow highway or representatives of clients were far more dangerous.

"They come up to a driver, show him all the necessary papers, and tell him to come with them to another customs terminal. After they finish the "paperwork' there, the driver finds out his truck has got much lighter," he said.
"Sometimes it is just completely empty."

He said his firm generally sends clients documents along with several Brazilian banknotes so that drivers, carrying copies of the same banknotes, can tell when he is talking to a genuine client with real documents.

"The road is the most dangerous thing," said another Russian importer. "Some firms prefer to find insurance companies, although there are not many of them. But many try to find other ways to secure their cargo."
"Sending trucks in convoy with armed security guards is probably the best," he concluded.

One driver, who travels to Finland and back twice a week, said that whenever he carries televisions or tobacco, his "co-driver" is a broad-shouldered individual with a pump-action Remington shotgun. He is not a driver at all.

"Normally there are two drivers in the cab, so that one doesn't get too tired. But I'd rather be exhausted than dead," he told Reuters. "They never attacked me, but I've heard lots of spooky stories from other drivers."

Robbers often use traffic police cars and uniforms to stop lone trucks. They are well armed and well equipped -- tracing the trucks along the route with the help of radio transceivers, sometimes using police frequencies.
One very common trick is putting a dummy on the road splashed with red ink, making the scene look like an accident.
"Some people stop and get killed or ripped off. If I saw that, I wouldn't even think of slowing down," the 25-year-old driver said.
